stem: On SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), what is the main purpose of the Cloud Connector?

options.text: To train models
To provide a secure outbound-initiated connection from BTP to systems in a customer's on-premise network without opening inbound firewall ports
To store vector embeddings
To replace the identity provider

explanation: The Cloud Connector runs in the customer network and opens an outbound tunnel to BTP so cloud applications can reach selected on-premise systems under controlled exposure. Destinations in the subaccount reference it.

stem: What does the "clean core" principle recommend for an ERP such as SAP S/4HANA when adding AI functions?

options.text: Modify standard code freely to embed AI logic
Keep the core standard and upgrade-safe by extending through released extension points and side-by-side applications on a platform
Avoid APIs
Move all data to a spreadsheet

explanation: Clean core keeps customisation out of the ERP core so upgrades stay simple; AI logic usually lives in side-by-side extensions calling released APIs and events.

stem: When is a pro-code approach to building an agent usually justified over a low-code studio?

options.text: When the agent is a simple, single-step automation for one business user
When you need complex orchestration, custom evaluation and testing, fine control over performance or integration patterns, and team-owned lifecycle management
When no developers are available
When you want no versioning

explanation: Low-code suits fast, bounded automations; pro-code is better when control, testability and complex logic are required. Many estates use both under shared governance.

stem: An AI agent running on BTP must read purchase orders from an on-premise ERP and must only return orders the signed-in buyer may see. The ERP is not reachable from the internet.
constraints: Authorisation must reflect the signed-in user
Audit must show which user triggered each call

options.text: Connect through the Cloud Connector with a destination in the subaccount, use principal propagation so the ERP evaluates the user's own authorisations, and log the user identity with each call.
Expose the ERP APIs publicly with an API key stored in the agent prompt.
Use one technical user with broad read access and filter results in the prompt.
Copy all purchase orders into a vector store and answer from it.

rationales.text: Principal propagation lets the ERP apply the real user's permissions.
Filtering results inside the prompt is a robust access control.
An outbound-initiated tunnel satisfies the no-inbound-exceptions rule.
Putting credentials in a prompt is acceptable if the agent is internal.

explanation: Reach on-premise systems via the connector pattern and keep authorisation with the system of record by propagating the user. A broad technical user plus prompt filtering moves the control into the model, which is not trustworthy.
model_answer: Use Cloud Connector and a destination for connectivity, propagate the user identity (principal propagation) so the ERP enforces entitlements, and write audit logs with user and agent identity.

rubric.criterion: Uses Cloud Connector or equivalent outbound tunnel
Rejects prompt-based filtering and embedded credentials

stem: Several SAP-centred teams each embed their own model-provider API key in their applications. Finance cannot see spend, security cannot rotate keys centrally, and models differ across teams.

options.text: Introduce a central model-access layer (for example a platform gateway or SAP's generative AI services where available to the client) with managed credentials, usage metering, approved models and policy controls, and migrate teams to it.
Document a policy asking teams to rotate keys quarterly.
Pick one model for the whole company and forbid others.
Let each team keep its keys and share spend by email.

rationales.text: A central layer gives one place for credentials, metering and policy.
A policy document enforces key hygiene without tooling.
Approved-model lists can still allow choice within governance.

explanation: Centralising model access gives visibility, credential control and policy enforcement while allowing governed choice. The product options available to a given client should be checked at the time of design.
model_answer: Create a model gateway or platform service, move credentials into managed secrets, meter by team, define approved models and data rules, and migrate.
